title: How Rape Kits Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain rape kits (sexual assault evidence collection kits): what they contain, their invention and history, the role of Marty Goddard and Chicago forensic investigator Vitullo, the Southwestern kit, recommended steps for victims, the exam process and consent, costs and billing, DNA databases (CODIS), the rape kit backlog across US cities, destruction of untested kits, reforms and funding, and the Joyful Heart Foundation's End the Backlog campaign. The episode opens with a trigger warning and ends with a listener mail segment about SMR (autonomous sensory meridian response) triggers.
topics: Southwestern Sexual Assault Evidence Collection Kit

segments.title: Trigger warning and opening remarks
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic with a trigger warning, note Sexual Assault Awareness Month and the April 2 Day of Action (wear teal), and state that sexual assault affects all genders and demographics, including men and trans people.

segments.title: What a rape kit is and its invention
segments.summary: A rape kit, also called a sexual assault evidence collection kit, is a box of supplies with step-by-step directions for collecting evidence. Kits began with the Chicago police, were called Vitullo kits, and were popularized by Chicago forensic investigator Vitullo. Marty Goddard is credited as the actual inventor.

segments.title: Marty Goddard and the Citizens for Victims Assistance
segments.summary: Marty Goddard, a sexual assault survivor, formed Citizens for Victims Assistance in the 1970s and worked to improve police handling of assault cases. The Playboy Foundation gave funding that helped assemble inexpensive kits. The Southwestern kit from Texas later became a model.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before the next section.

segments.title: Why evidence collection matters and steps to take after an assault
segments.summary: Sexual assault victims' bodies are crime scenes. Experts recommend going to an emergency room within about 24 hours (evidence viable up to three days), not showering, keeping or bagging clothing, and possibly placing paper or towel down when changing. Reporting to police is not required at the exam, and a Jane Doe exam is possible. Statutes of limitations vary by state.

segments.title: The exam process, consent, and SANE nurses
segments.summary: The exam is invasive and takes hours. Patients are asked for consent before each step and about history, drugs or drinking. Samples include blood, urine, scalp hair, mouth swabs and pubic hair combings. Sexual assault nurse examiners (SANEs) are available in major cities but rarer in rural areas. Chuck and Josh discuss the need for funding.

segments.title: Costs, billing, and the chain of custody
segments.summary: The kit exam itself is not charged, but treatment for injuries, STD medication, and emergency contraception may be billed. Josh criticizes this and notes pre-Affordable Care Act insurance denials for prior rape. The sealed kit goes to law enforcement with signatures for chain of custody.

segments.title: CODIS and the rape kit backlog
segments.summary: Kits are tested in DNA labs and checked against CODIS. Untested kits were found in warehouses across the country beginning in the 2000s, including large counts in Detroit, Memphis, Dallas, Phoenix and Akron. Recidivism is discussed. Congress funded roughly 150 million dollars to clear the backlog, but cops and follow-up were also needed.

segments.title: Reforms, destroyed kits, and the End the Backlog campaign
segments.summary: Federal and state reforms include the SAFER Act of 2013 and New York timelines. Fayetteville, North Carolina police destroyed about 300 untested kits, and CNN found other agencies had destroyed kits. The Justice Department suggests holding kits for at least 50 years or the statute of limitations. Mariska Hargitay's Joyful Heart Foundation runs End the Backlog.

segments.title: Recent news cases from rape kit testing
segments.summary: Hosts describe recent cases: Austin police testing about 27 kits with grant money, a Tucson man convicted of raping seven women after a grant-funded test, and an Orlando man found in Puerto Rico after a kit was tested.

segments.title: Listener mail: SMR triggers
segments.summary: A listener mail segment about autonomous sensory meridian response (SMR) triggers such as paint roller sounds, Bob Ross painting videos, and swallowing sounds. Josh and Chuck discuss artists painting slowly.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contacts and point listeners to the website for more information.
